arXiv:2506.03646v3 [math.CO] 05 Jun 2026

A Note on Inequalities for Three Domination Parameters

Dickson Y. B. Annor 55 5 Department of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, La Trobe University, Bendigo, Australia ( d.annor@latrobe.edu.au). Research of Annor supported by a La Trobe Graduate Research Scholarship.
Abstract

In this short paper, we establish relations between the domination number γ\gamma, the total domination number γt\gamma_{t}, and the connected domination number γc\gamma_{c} of a graph. In particular, we prove upper and lower bounds for γt\gamma_{t} in terms of γ\gamma and γc\gamma_{c}.

Keywords: domination, total domination, connected domination.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C69.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we deal with finite undirected and simple graphs. For a graph GG, let V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) respectively denote the vertex set and the edge set of GG.

Let SS be a subset of the vertex set of a graph GG. SS is called a dominating set of GG if every vertex not in SS is adjacent to at least one vertex in SS. The domination number of FF, denoted by γ⁡(G)\gamma(G), is the minimum cardinality of a dominating set of FF. A total dominating set of GG is a set SS such that every vertex is adjacent to some vertex in SS. Note that by the definition of a total dominating set, it is evident that a graph GG admits a total dominating set if and only if GG has no isolated vertices. The total domination number of GG, denoted by γt​(G)\gamma_{t}(G), is the minimum cardinality of a total dominating set of GG. A connected dominating set SS of GG is a set such that every vertex not in SS is adjacent with at least one vertex in SS and the subgraph induced by SS is connected. The connected domination number γc​(G)\gamma_{c}(G) is the minimum cardinality of a connected dominating set of GG. Note that a graph admits a connected dominating set if and only if the graph is connected.

The theory of domination in graphs is one of the main research areas in graph theory. In 1979, Bollobás and Cockayne [1] observed that the total domination number of an isolate-free graph is squeezed between the domination number and twice the domination number.

Theorem 1 ([1]).

If GG is an isolated-free graph, then γ⁡(G)⩽γt​(G)⩽2​γ​(G)\gamma(G)\leqslant\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 2\gamma(G).

It is obvious that a connected dominating set is a dominating set. Sampathkumar and Walikar [6] proved the following result.

Theorem 2 ([6]).

If GG is a connected graph, then γ⁡(G)⩽γc​(G)⩽3​γ​(G)−2\gamma(G)\leqslant\gamma_{c}(G)\leqslant 3\gamma(G)-2.

The following easy fact was observed in [5].

Fact 1.

If GG is a connected isolated-free graph and γ⁡(G)>1\gamma(G)>1, then γ⁡(G)⩽γt​(G)⩽γc​(G)\gamma(G)\leqslant\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant\gamma_{c}(G).

A natural question is: what relationships exist between γ,γt\gamma,\gamma_{t} and γc\gamma_{c}?

To our knowledge, little or nothing is known about the relations between γ,γt\gamma,\gamma_{t} and γc\gamma_{c}, (and moreover, any three domination parameters in general). This motivates us to study the relationships between γ​(G),γt​(G)\gamma(G),\gamma_{t}(G) and γc​(G)\gamma_{c}(G) when GG is a connected isolated-free graph.

For an excellent treatment of fundamentals of domination in graphs and recent topics on bounds for these three domination parameters, we refer the reader to the following books [4, 3, 2].

2 Main results

In this section, we demonstrate some relationships and show that these results are best possible.

Theorem 3.

If GG is a connected isolated-free graph and γ⁡(G)>1\gamma(G)>1, then

γt​(G)⩽γ⁡(G)+12​γc​(G).\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant\gamma(G)+\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{c}(G).

Moreover, this bound is tight.

Proof.

Let GG be a connected isolated-free graph with γ⁡(G)>1\gamma(G)>1. From Theorem 1 and Fact 1, we have γt​(G)⩽2​γ​(G)\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 2\gamma(G) and γt​(G)⩽γc​(G)\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant\gamma_{c}(G), respectively. By adding these two inequalities, we get 2​γt​(G)⩽2​γ​(G)+γc​(G)2\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 2\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G) and the result follows immediately. In Figure 1, it can easily be checked that γ⁡(H)=5\gamma(H)=5 and γt​(H)=γc​(H)=10\gamma_{t}(H)=\gamma_{c}(H)=10, which proves that the bound is tight. ∎

Similarly, we can deduce the following result from Theorems 1 and 2.

Theorem 4.

If GG is a connected isolated-free graph, then

γt​(G)⩽5​γ​(G)−γc​(G)−2.\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 5\gamma(G)-\gamma_{c}(G)-2.

Moreover, this bound is tight.

Equality in Theorem 4 is achieved for complete graphs. In fact, the following generalisation of Theorem 3 holds for all connected isolated-free graphs.

Theorem 5.

For any connected isolated-free graph GG,

γt​(G)⩽⌈2​(γ⁡(G)+γc​(G))3⌉.\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant\left\lceil\frac{2(\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G))}{3}\right\rceil.

Moreover, this bound is tight.

Proof.

Let GG be a connected isolated-free graph. If γ⁡(G)>1\gamma(G)>1, then it follows from Fact 1 that 2​γt​(G)⩽2​γc​(G)2\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 2\gamma_{c}(G). So, by Theorem 1, we have

2​γt​(G)+γt​(G)⩽2​γ​(G)+2​γc​(G)⇒γt​(G)⩽2​(γ⁡(G)+γc​(G))3.2\gamma_{t}(G)+\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant 2\gamma(G)+2\gamma_{c}(G)\Rightarrow\gamma_{t}(G)\leqslant\frac{2(\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G))}{3}.

On the other hand, if γ⁡(G)=1\gamma(G)=1, then GG has a dominant vertex. That is, GG has a vertex that dominates every other vertex of GG. In that case, γt​(G)=2\gamma_{t}(G)=2. So, ⌈2×23⌉=2\lceil\frac{2\times 2}{3}\rceil=2. Furthermore, this proves that the bound is tight. ∎

Now we turn our attention to the lower bounds. First, we point out the following lower bound, which is a consequence of Theorems 1 and 2.

Proposition 6.

If GG is a connected isolated-free graph, then

γt​(G)⩾2​γ​(G)−γc​(G).\gamma_{t}(G)\geqslant 2\gamma(G)-\gamma_{c}(G).

Moreover, this bound is tight.

Remark 1.

Equality is achieved for the graph G′G^{\prime} in Figure 2.

Finally, we end this section by proving the following bound.

Theorem 7.

For every connected isolated-free graph GG,

γt​(G)⩾⌊3​γ​(G)+γc​(G)6⌋.\gamma_{t}(G)\geqslant\left\lfloor\frac{3\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G)}{6}\right\rfloor.
Proof.

Suppose not. Then γt​(G)<⌊3​γ​(G)+γc​(G)6⌋\gamma_{t}(G)<\left\lfloor\frac{3\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G)}{6}\right\rfloor, which implies that γt​(G)<3​γ​(G)+γc​(G)6\gamma_{t}(G)<\frac{3\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G)}{6} because γt​(G)∈ℕ\gamma_{t}(G)\in\mathbb{N}. Applying Theorem 2, we get

6​γt​(G)<3​γ​(G)+γc​(G)⩽3​γ​(G)+3​γ​(G)−2=6​γ​(G)−2.6\gamma_{t}(G)<3\gamma(G)+\gamma_{c}(G)\leqslant 3\gamma(G)+3\gamma(G)-2=6\gamma(G)-2.

Once again, Theorem 1 implies that 6​γ​(G)⩽6​γt​(G)<6​γ​(G)−26\gamma(G)\leqslant 6\gamma_{t}(G)<6\gamma(G)-2; a contradiction. ∎

3 Conclusion

In this paper, we established relationships between γ​(G),γt​(G)\gamma(G),\gamma_{t}(G) and γc​(G)\gamma_{c}(G) for a connected isolated-free graph GG.
